In [[set theory]],  an [[ordinal number]] ''α'' is an '''admissible ordinal''' if [[constructible universe|L<sub>''α''</sub>]] is an [[admissible set]] (that is, a [[Inner model|transitive model]] of [[Kripke–Platek set theory]]); in other words, ''α'' is admissible when ''α'' is a [[limit ordinal]] and L<sub>''α''</sub> ⊧ Σ<sub>0</sub>-collection.<ref name="friedman">{{citation
 | last = Friedman | first = Sy D.|authorlink = Sy Friedman
 | contribution = Fine structure theory and its applications
 | doi = 10.1090/pspum/042/791062
 | mr = 791062
 | pages = 259–269
 | publisher = Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI
 | series = Proc. Sympos. Pure Math.
 | title = Recursion theory (Ithaca, N.Y., 1982)
 | volume = 42
 | year = 1985}}. See in particular [https://books.google.com/books?id=2vvg3mRzDtwC&pg=PA265 p.&nbsp;265].</ref><ref name="fitting">{{citation
 | last = Fitting | first = Melvin|authorlink = Melvin Fitting
 | isbn = 0-444-86171-8
 | mr = 644315
 | page = 238
 | publisher = North-Holland Publishing Co., Amsterdam-New York
 | series = Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics
 | title = Fundamentals of generalized recursion theory
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=GRE7AAAAQBAJ&pg=PA238
 | volume = 105
 | year = 1981}}.</ref> The term was coined by Richard Platek in 1966.<ref>G. E. Sacks, [https://projecteuclid.org/ebook/Download?urlId=pl%2F1235422639&isFullBook=False ''Higher Recursion Theory''] (p.151). Association for Symbolic Logic, ''Perspectives in Logic''</ref>

The first two admissible ordinals are ω and <math>\omega_1^{\mathrm{CK}}</math> (the least [[nonrecursive ordinal]], also called the [[Church–Kleene ordinal]]).<ref name="fitting"/>  Any [[regular cardinal|regular]] [[uncountable]] [[cardinal number|cardinal]] is an admissible ordinal.

By a theorem of [[Gerald Sacks|Sacks]], the [[countable set|countable]] admissible ordinals are exactly those constructed in a manner similar to the Church–Kleene ordinal, but for [[Turing machine]]s with [[Oracle machine|oracles]].<ref name="friedman"/>  One sometimes writes <math>\omega_\alpha^{\mathrm{CK}}</math> for the <math>\alpha</math>-th ordinal that is either admissible or a limit of admissibles; an ordinal that is both is called ''recursively inaccessible''.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Friedman | first = Sy D.
 | contribution = Constructibility and class forcing
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4020-5764-9_9
 | mr = 2768687
 | pages = 557–604
 | publisher = Springer, Dordrecht
 | title = Handbook of set theory. Vols. 1, 2, 3
 | year = 2010}}. See in particular [https://books.google.com/books?id=DLCyehuI0i0C&pg=PA560 p.&nbsp;560].</ref> There exists a theory of large ordinals in this manner that is highly parallel to that of (small) [[large cardinal property|large cardinals]] (one can define recursively [[Mahlo cardinal|Mahlo]] ordinals, for example).<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Kahle | first1 = Reinhard
 | last2 = Setzer | first2 = Anton
 | contribution = An extended predicative definition of the Mahlo universe
 | mr = 2883363
 | pages = 315–340
 | publisher = Ontos Verlag, Heusenstamm
 | series = Ontos Math. Log.
 | title = Ways of proof theory
 | volume = 2
 | year = 2010}}.</ref> But all these ordinals are still countable. Therefore, admissible ordinals seem to be the recursive analogue of regular [[cardinal number]]s.

Notice that ''α'' is an admissible ordinal if and only if ''α'' is a [[limit ordinal]] and there does not exist a ''γ'' &lt; ''α'' for which there is a Σ<sub>1</sub>(L<sub>''α''</sub>) mapping from ''γ'' onto ''α''.<ref>[[Keith Devlin|K. Devlin]], [https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/30905237.pdf An introduction to the fine structure of the constructible hierarchy] (1974) (p.38). Accessed 2021-05-06.</ref> <math>\alpha</math> is an admissible ordinal if and only if there is a standard model <math>M</math> of KP whose set of ordinals is <math>\alpha</math>, in fact this may be take as the definition of admissibility.<ref>K. J. Devlin, ''Constructibility'' (1984), ch. 2, "The Constructible Universe, p.95. Perspectives in Mathematical Logic, Springer-Verlag.</ref><ref name="Barwise76">[[John Barwise|J. Barwise]], ''Admissible Sets and Structures'' (1976). Cambridge University Press</ref> The <math>\alpha</math>th admissible ordinal is sometimes denoted by <math>\tau_\alpha</math><ref>P. G. Hinman, ''Recursion-Theoretic Hierarchies'' (1978), pp.419--420. Perspectives in Mathematical Logic, ISBN 3-540-07904-1.</ref><ref name="Barwise76" /><sup>p.&nbsp;174</sup> or <math>\tau^0_\alpha</math>.<ref>{{cite conference |author-link1=Saul Kripke |first=Saul |last=Kripke |url=https://saulkripkecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Transfinite-Recursion-Constructible-Sets-and-Analogues-of-Cardinals-PUBLIC.pdf |title=Transfinite Recursion, Constructible Sets, and Analogues of Cardinals |year=1967 |access-date=2023-07-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240416012536/https://saulkripkecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Transfinite-Recursion-Constructible-Sets-and-Analogues-of-Cardinals-PUBLIC.pdf |archive-date=2024-04-16}}</ref>

The Friedman–Jensen–Sacks theorem states that a countable <math>\alpha</math> is admissible if and only if there exists some <math>A\subseteq\omega</math> such that <math>\alpha</math> is the least ordinal not recursive in <math>A</math>.<ref>W. Marek, M. Srebrny, "[https://philpapers.org/rec/MARGIT-4 Gaps in the Constructible Universe]" (1973), pp.361--362. Annals of Mathematical Logic 6</ref> Equivalently, for any countable admissible <math>\alpha</math>, there is an <math>A\subseteq\mathbb N</math> making <math>\alpha</math> minimal such that <math>\langle L_\alpha, \in, A\rangle</math> is an admissible structure.<ref>[[Alexander S. Kechris|A. S. Kechris]], "[https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1975-202-00/S0002-9947-1975-0419235-7/S0002-9947-1975-0419235-7.pdf The Theory of Countable Analytical Sets]"</ref><sup>p. 264</sup>
